text: Last lesson ended on a real limitation: give a Service type LoadBalancer and your cloud provider provisions a dedicated external load balancer for it, billed on its own. Fine for one app, expensive for ten. This lesson is about Ingress, which routes HTTP and HTTPS traffic to many backend Services through one shared entry point instead of one cloud load balancer per app.

Here's the part that trips people up: an Ingress resource by itself does nothing. It's a declarative description of routing rules, not a running process. Something has to watch for Ingress objects and actually implement them — that's an Ingress controller, like ingress-nginx or Traefik, usually running as Pods fronted by exactly one LoadBalancer Service. Every Ingress rides behind that single external IP, and each rule still points at an ordinary backend Service underneath.

This Ingress routes requests for api.example.com with a path starting in /payments to the payments-api Service, on port 80, using pathType Prefix. ingressClassName: nginx tells Kubernetes which installed controller should pick up this object, which matters once a cluster has more than one. Add another rule block for /orders pointed at a different Service, and both now share this same front door.

Ingress is also the usual place to terminate HTTPS. The tls section's secretName points at a kubernetes.io/tls Secret holding the certificate and private key for that host. The Ingress controller decrypts HTTPS right there at the shared entry point and forwards plain HTTP on to the backend Service — so individual Services never have to handle certificates themselves.

Two commands you'll use constantly: kubectl get ingress shows the host, an ADDRESS column once the controller's external IP is assigned, and the ports in use. kubectl describe ingress is the more useful one day to day — it prints every rule next to the exact backend Service and port it resolves to, which is exactly what you check first when a route isn't reaching where you expected.

So far every example has pointed at a Service by name — payments-api, orders-api — and trusted Kubernetes to resolve that name to the right place. Next lesson opens up exactly how that resolution works: CoreDNS, and the full service.namespace.svc.cluster.local naming scheme every Pod in the cluster can use.
